title: Lindblad Dynamics
intro: When a reservoir decays, dephases or is pumped continuously, its evolution in time is a Lindblad (GKSL) master equation. This page builds that equation from small channels, solves it for one qubit (T1 and T2), writes it as a matrix whose spectrum gives the relaxation rates and the steady state, and turns the gap into a reservoir's memory time.

blocks.text: What you need first

The previous page, Density Matrices and Channels (#/qrc/open-systems/density-matrices-and-channels), introduced density matrices and channels, including amplitude damping and dephasing as maps with a parameter $\gamma$ or $p$. This page needs those, the Schrödinger equation from The Schrödinger Equation (#/quantum/dynamics/schrodinger-equation), and the idea of an eigenvalue from Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors (#/quantum/foundations/eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors). The chapter Getting Started (#/qrc/start) gave the reservoir step in discrete time; here we see where the channel of a step comes from when the physics runs continuously.
What you will be able to do

items: Write a Lindblad master equation for a qubit or a few qubits and say what each term does.
Derive the T1 and T2 decay laws from the equation and explain why $T_2\le2T_1$.
Build the Liouvillian as a matrix in numpy, find its steady state, and read the relaxation time from its gap.
Convert a continuous decay rate into the damping parameter of one reservoir step and into a memory length measured in steps.
Explain what a quantum trajectory is and why its average reproduces the master equation.

blocks.text: From a decay law to a master equation
Why we need it

The channels of the previous page came with a single number, $\gamma$ or $p$, that said how much damping happened in one go. In a real device, damping is a process in time: the longer you wait, the more of it there is. We need an equation that says how the state changes in each small instant, and that is guaranteed to give a valid channel at every time. The closed-system version is the Schrödinger equation $\dot{\vert\psi\rangle}=-iH\vert\psi\rangle$ (units with $\hbar=1$), or for density matrices $\dot\rho=-i[H,\rho]$. The open-system version has extra terms for what the environment does.
The idea in plain words

Think of a bucket with a small leak. The water level falls at a rate proportional to how much water is in it, $\dot h=-h/\tau$, so the level decays exponentially with a time constant $\tau$. The leak does not care how long the bucket has been leaking, only how much is in it now: the process has no memory. That 'no memory' property is called the Markov property, and an excited qubit radiating into its surroundings behaves in the same way: in each short interval $dt$ it has a probability $\gamma\,dt$ of decaying, whatever happened before. The analogy breaks on one point. A leaking bucket stays a bucket; a qubit decaying also loses its phase information, in a way that is tied to the population loss by the quantum mechanics of the process. The equation below gets both right.
The maths: a channel for a very short time

Take a short time $dt$ and ask what Kraus operators describe what happens to the system. Two things can happen: either nothing detectable occurs, and the state evolves under the Hamiltonian with a slight shrinking of the amplitude, or a 'jump' occurs, an abrupt event such as a photon emission. A jump is described by an operator $L$, the jump operator, and occurs with a probability proportional to $dt$. So we choose

blocks.caption: Kraus operators for a short time $dt$: no jump ($K_0$), and a jump ($K_1$). $\gamma\ge0$ is the rate.

blocks.text: Check that this is a valid channel to first order in $dt$. $K_0^\dagger K_0=I+\big(iH-iH-\gamma L^\dagger L\big)dt+O(dt^2)=I-\gamma L^\dagger L\,dt$ (the two Hamiltonian terms cancel because $H$ is Hermitian, and the $L^\dagger L$ terms add). And $K_1^\dagger K_1=\gamma\,dt\,L^\dagger L$. The sum is $I$ ✓. The 'no jump' operator carries a piece $-\tfrac12\gamma L^\dagger L\,dt$ with a precise purpose: it is exactly the shrinkage needed so that the total probability stays 1, and it means that not seeing a jump is itself information, as the trajectory picture below makes concrete.
Now apply the channel to $\rho$ and keep terms to first order in $dt$:

items: $K_0\rho K_0^\dagger=\rho-i[H,\rho]\,dt-\tfrac12\gamma\big(L^\dagger L\rho+\rho L^\dagger L\big)dt$, where $[H,\rho]=H\rho-\rho H$ comes from the $-iH\,dt$ on each side.
$K_1\rho K_1^\dagger=\gamma\,dt\,L\rho L^\dagger$.
Add them and move $\rho$ to the left: $\dfrac{\rho(t+dt)-\rho(t)}{dt}=-i[H,\rho]+\gamma\Big(L\rho L^\dagger-\tfrac12L^\dagger L\rho-\tfrac12\rho L^\dagger L\Big)$.

blocks.text: With several channels of loss, each with its own $L_j$ and rate $\gamma_j$, the terms add. The result is the master equation of Gorini, Kossakowski, Sudarshan and Lindblad (GKSL, or just Lindblad):

blocks.caption: The Lindblad equation. The first term is the unitary part. Each $j$ is a dissipator, one kind of environment action. $\mathcal L$ is called the Lindbladian or Liouvillian.

blocks.text: Doing $N$ short steps of length $dt=t/N$ in a row gives $(1+\mathcal L\,dt)^N\to e^{t\mathcal L}$ as $N\to\infty$, so the solution is $\rho(t)=e^{t\mathcal L}\rho(0)$. The family $\mathcal E_t=e^{t\mathcal L}$ has the semigroup property $\mathcal E_{t+u}=\mathcal E_t\mathcal E_u$ (a process without memory), and the theorem of Lindblad and of Gorini–Kossakowski–Sudarshan says the converse: any semigroup of channels has a generator of exactly this form, with $\gamma_j\ge0$. The condition $\gamma_j\ge0$ is what makes every $e^{t\mathcal L}$ completely positive.

The equation is derived for a system weakly coupled to a large bath under three approximations. The Born approximation: the coupling is weak, so the bath is not changed by the system. The Markov approximation: the bath forgets any disturbance much faster than the system changes, so there is no memory. The secular approximation: terms that rotate fast compared with the relaxation are dropped. Where they fail (strongly coupled or structured environments) the evolution is not a semigroup and the equation is not valid. A common mistake is to write $-\tfrac12\{L^\dagger L,\rho\}$ as a free choice: it is not; without it the trace is not conserved, since $\operatorname{Tr}(L\rho L^\dagger)=\operatorname{Tr}(L^\dagger L\rho)$ and the three dissipator terms cancel exactly in the trace.
The common jump operators

items: Energy loss ($T_1$ decay): $L=\sigma^-=\vert0\rangle\langle1\vert$ at rate $\gamma_1$. Takes the excited state $\vert1\rangle$ to $\vert0\rangle$. (The convention here: $\vert0\rangle$ is the ground state, $Z=+1$.)
Pure dephasing: $L=Z$ at rate $\gamma_\varphi/2$. Does not change populations; the dissipator reduces to $Z\rho Z-\rho$.
Heating (absorption): $L=\sigma^+=\vert1\rangle\langle0\vert$ at rate $\gamma_\uparrow$.
Depolarising: all three of $X,Y,Z$ at equal rates.

blocks.title: Check yourself: trace of the dissipator
blocks.text: Show that $\operatorname{Tr}\mathcal L(\rho)=0$ for every $\rho$, which is why the trace stays 1.
solution: $\operatorname{Tr}(L^\dagger L\rho)$ and $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho L^\dagger L)$ are equal, so the three terms give $1-\tfrac12-\tfrac12=0$.
blocks.answer: The three dissipator terms contribute $+\operatorname{Tr}(L^\dagger L\rho)-\tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}(L^\dagger L\rho)-\tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}(L^\dagger L\rho)=0$; the commutator has zero trace

blocks.text: One qubit: T1 and T2
The equations of motion

Write $\rho$ with entries $\rho_{00},\rho_{01},\rho_{10},\rho_{11}$, take $H=\tfrac\omega2Z$ (a qubit with energy splitting $\omega$), and use the two dissipators: $L_1=\sigma^-$ at rate $\gamma_1=1/T_1$ and $L_2=Z$ at rate $\gamma_\varphi/2$. We need each dissipator's action on the entries.

items: Hamiltonian part. $-i[H,\rho]$ with $H=\tfrac\omega2Z$: the entry $(j,k)$ of $H\rho-\rho H$ is $(h_j-h_k)\rho_{jk}$ with $h_0=\omega/2$, $h_1=-\omega/2$. So populations are unchanged and $\dot\rho_{01}=-i\omega\rho_{01}$: the coherence rotates at frequency $\omega$ (its modulus stays).

Relaxation $\sigma^-$. Here $\sigma^-\rho\sigma^+=\rho_{11}\vert0\rangle\langle0\vert$ and $\sigma^+\sigma^-=\vert1\rangle\langle1\vert$. The term $-\tfrac12\{\vert1\rangle\langle1\vert,\rho\}$ has entries $(1,1)$: $-\rho_{11}$; $(0,1)$ and $(1,0)$: $-\tfrac12\rho_{01}$, $-\tfrac12\rho_{10}$; $(0,0)$: 0. Total: $\dot\rho_{00}=+\gamma_1\rho_{11}$, $\dot\rho_{11}=-\gamma_1\rho_{11}$, $\dot\rho_{01}=-\tfrac12\gamma_1\rho_{01}$.

Dephasing $Z$ with rate $g=\gamma_\varphi/2$. $Z\rho Z$ equals $\rho$ on the diagonal and $-\rho$ on the off-diagonal; and $-\tfrac12\{Z^2,\rho\}=-\rho$. So the dissipator gives $0$ on the diagonal and $-2\rho_{01}$ on the coherence: $\dot\rho_{01}=-2g\rho_{01}=-\gamma_\varphi\rho_{01}$.

blocks.text: All the ingredients are decoupled linear equations with the solutions

blocks.caption: Populations relax at $1/T_1$, coherences at $1/T_2$. $T_\varphi=1/\gamma_\varphi$ is the pure-dephasing time.

blocks.text: The bound $T_2\le2T_1$ follows at once, since $1/T_\varphi\ge0$. It is not a convention. The coherence $\rho_{01}$ is a product of two amplitudes, one for $\vert0\rangle$ and one for $\vert1\rangle$. The excited amplitude decays at half the rate of the probability (probability is amplitude squared), so even without any extra noise the coherence decays at $\gamma_1/2$. Extra dephasing can only add to that.
Worked example
A qubit with $T_1=50$ and $T_2=40$ (microseconds), starting in $\vert+\rangle$, so $\rho_{11}(0)=\tfrac12$ and $\vert\rho_{01}(0)\vert=\tfrac12$.

items: Step 1. $1/T_\varphi=1/T_2-1/(2T_1)=1/40-1/100=0.015$ per microsecond, so $T_\varphi=66.7$.
Step 4. The expectation $\langle Z\rangle=\rho_{00}-\rho_{11}=1-2\rho_{11}=0.330$. It started at 0 and is climbing to $+1$ as the qubit relaxes to $\vert0\rangle$.
Step 5. Read both off the code below, which builds the Liouvillian of the next section for these numbers and prints the same values.

widget.title: A qubit under T1 and T2

blocks.text: Try this. (1) Leave the defaults ($T_1=50$, $T_2=40$, $\theta=90^\circ$). The population curve starts at 0.5 and decays; $\langle Z\rangle$ starts at 0 and rises toward 1; the coherence starts at 0.5 and has fallen to $0.5/e=0.18$ by time 40. (2) Set $T_2=100$: this is $2T_1$, pure relaxation with no extra dephasing, and the coherence decays as slowly as it can, reaching $0.18$ at time 100. (3) Set $T_2=10$ with $T_1=50$: the coherence collapses within a few tens of time units while $\rho_{11}$ and $\langle Z\rangle$ do not change at all, because dephasing never touches populations. (4) Set $\theta=180^\circ$ (the state $\vert1\rangle$): the coherence curve is flat zero (there is no superposition), and $\langle Z\rangle=1-2e^{-t/50}$ crosses zero at $50\ln2=34.7$, the time at which half the population has decayed. A reservoir read out only through $\langle Z\rangle$ sees $T_1$ directly, and sees $T_2$ only through whatever the coupling Hamiltonian converts from coherence into populations.

A scale to keep in mind. On superconducting qubits $T_1$ and $T_2$ are typically tens to hundreds of microseconds against gate times of tens of nanoseconds. It is that ratio, not $T_1$ itself, that fixes how many reservoir steps fit before natural noise has erased the state: with a 1 microsecond step, $T_1=50$ microseconds is 50 steps.
From a rate to one reservoir step

A reservoir step lasting $\Delta t$ applies the channel $e^{\Delta t\mathcal L}$. For the damping alone, comparing with the amplitude-damping channel of the previous page, whose excited population is multiplied by $1-\gamma$, shows that the discrete parameter is $\gamma=1-e^{-\Delta t/T_1}$. Dephasing multiplies the coherence by $1-2p$, so $1-2p=e^{-\Delta t/T_\varphi}$. For small $\Delta t/T_1$ these are $\gamma\approx\Delta t/T_1$ and $p\approx\Delta t/(2T_\varphi)$. With $\Delta t=1$ and $T_1=50$: $\gamma=1-e^{-0.02}=0.0198$, almost exactly $\Delta t/T_1=0.02$.

blocks.title: Check yourself: per-step damping
blocks.text: A step lasts $\Delta t=1\ \mu s$ on a qubit with $T_1=50\ \mu s$ and $T_2=40\ \mu s$. What is the coherence factor per step, and what dephasing probability $p$ does that correspond to?
blocks.hint: Use the total coherence decay time $T_2$, not $T_1$.
solution: The coherence decays at $1/T_2$ in total (both effects), so the factor per step is $e^{-\Delta t/T_2}=e^{-0.025}=0.9753$.
Written as a dephasing alone, $1-2p=0.9753$, so $p=0.0123$. (The amplitude-damping channel alone already contributes $\sqrt{1-\gamma}=0.9901$ to this factor; the rest is extra dephasing.)

blocks.text: The Liouvillian as a matrix
Why we need it

For one qubit we could solve by hand. For two or more qubits, with Hamiltonians coupling them, we need a systematic method, and the observation that makes one possible is that $\mathcal L$ is a linear map on matrices, so it is a matrix once we stack the entries of $\rho$ into a vector.
The maths

Stack the rows of $\rho$ one after another into a vector $\operatorname{vec}(\rho)$ of length $d^2$ (row-major order, as numpy's reshape does). If $\rho$ has entries $\rho_{kl}$, then the entry of $A\rho B$ at position $(i,j)$ is $\sum_{k,l}A_{ik}\rho_{kl}B_{lj}$. As a map on the stacked vector, that is a matrix whose entry at row $(i,j)$, column $(k,l)$ is $A_{ik}B_{lj}$, which is exactly the Kronecker product $A\otimes B^\top$. So $\operatorname{vec}(A\rho B)=(A\otimes B^\top)\operatorname{vec}(\rho)$. Apply it to each term:

items: $H\rho$ is $A=H$, $B=I$: matrix $H\otimes I$. $\rho H$ is $A=I$, $B=H$: matrix $I\otimes H^\top$.
$L\rho L^\dagger$: $A=L$, $B=L^\dagger$, so $B^\top=L^*$ (the element-wise complex conjugate): matrix $L\otimes L^*$.
$L^\dagger L\rho$: $(L^\dagger L)\otimes I$. $\rho L^\dagger L$: $I\otimes(L^\dagger L)^\top$.

blocks.tex: \hat{\mathcal L}=-i\big(H\otimes I-I\otimes H^\top\big)+\sum_j\gamma_j\Big(L_j\otimes L_j^*-\tfrac12L_j^\dagger L_j\otimes I-\tfrac12I\otimes(L_j^\dagger L_j)^\top\Big)
blocks.caption: The Liouvillian as a $d^2\times d^2$ matrix; $\operatorname{vec}\rho(t)=e^{t\hat{\mathcal L}}\operatorname{vec}\rho(0)$.

blocks.text: What its eigenvalues mean

items: Real parts are $\le0$. The matrices $e^{t\hat{\mathcal L}}$ are channels, and channels never increase the distance between states (the next page, Contraction and Fixed Points (#/qrc/open-systems/contraction-and-fixed-points), proves it), so nothing can grow exponentially.

There is at least one eigenvalue $0$. Since $\operatorname{Tr}\mathcal L(\rho)=0$ for every $\rho$, the row vector $\operatorname{vec}(I)^\top$ (which computes the trace) satisfies $\operatorname{vec}(I)^\top\hat{\mathcal L}=0$, so $0$ is an eigenvalue and a right eigenvector exists too. The right eigenvector, normalised to unit trace, is a steady state $\rho_{\mathrm{ss}}$, with $\mathcal L(\rho_{\mathrm{ss}})=0$.
Complex eigenvalues come in conjugate pairs ($\mathcal L$ maps Hermitian matrices to Hermitian matrices). The imaginary parts are oscillation frequencies of the relaxation.

If the zero eigenvalue is unique, every initial state converges to $\rho_{\mathrm{ss}}$: $\rho(t)=\rho_{\mathrm{ss}}+\sum_kc_ke^{\lambda_kt}R_k$ with coefficients $c_k$ fixed by the initial state. The slowest approach is at the Liouvillian gap $g=-\max_{k\ge1}\operatorname{Re}\lambda_k$.

blocks.text: For a reservoir, $1/g$ is the longest time over which any trace of the initial state or of old inputs survives: the memory horizon. If $g$ is too large, the reservoir forgets faster than the task needs. If $g$ is too small, it remembers the initial state and old inputs for too long, the washout (the initial stretch discarded before training, see Training, Testing and Measuring Error (#/qrc/start/training-and-testing)) must be long, and old inputs contaminate the new ones.
Worked example: the one-qubit spectrum

For the qubit above with $T_1=50$, $T_2=40$, $\omega=0.2$, the matrix is $4\times4$. Its eigenvalues are what we found by hand: $0$ (the steady state, $\vert0\rangle\langle0\vert$), $-1/T_1=-0.02$ (the population mode), and the pair $-1/T_2\pm i\omega=-0.025\pm0.2i$ (the two coherences). The code below finds all of these numerically.

blocks.source:
import numpy as np
from scipy.linalg import expm
I = np.eye(2); X = np.array([[0, 1], [1, 0]]); Z = np.diag([1., -1])
sm = np.array([[0, 1], [0, 0]])           # sigma^- = |0><1|: |1> is the excited state

def liouvillian(H, jumps):
    """Row-major vectorisation: vec(A rho B) = (A kron B^T) vec(rho)."""
    d = H.shape[0]; Id = np.eye(d)
    L = -1j * (np.kron(H, Id) - np.kron(Id, H.T))
    for c in jumps:
        cdc = c.conj().T @ c
        L += np.kron(c, c.conj()) - 0.5 * np.kron(cdc, Id) - 0.5 * np.kron(Id, cdc.T)
    return L

T1, T2, w = 50.0, 40.0, 0.2
g1 = 1 / T1; gphi = 1 / T2 - 1 / (2 * T1)          # 1/T2 = 1/(2 T1) + 1/Tphi
H = 0.5 * w * Z                                    # H = omega Z / 2
L = liouvillian(H, [np.sqrt(g1) * sm, np.sqrt(gphi / 2) * Z])
ev = np.linalg.eigvals(L); ev = ev[np.argsort(-ev.real)]
print("1/T1 = %.4f, 1/T2 = %.4f, 1/Tphi = %.4f" % (g1, 1 / T2, gphi))
print("Liouvillian eigenvalues:", np.round(ev, 4))
rho0 = np.array([[0.5, 0.5], [0.5, 0.5]])         # |+><+|
for t in [0, 20, 40, 100]:
    r = (expm(L * t) @ rho0.reshape(-1)).reshape(2, 2)
    print(f"t={t:3d}: rho11 = {r[1,1].real:.4f}  |rho01| = {abs(r[0,1]):.4f}   (formulas {0.5*np.exp(-t/T1):.4f}, {0.5*np.exp(-t/T2):.4f})")

blocks.text: The program prints: 1/T1 = 0.0200, 1/T2 = 0.0250, 1/Tphi = 0.0150, and the four eigenvalues $0$, $-0.02$, $-0.025\mp0.2i$ as predicted. At times 0, 20, 40, 100 the matrix exponential gives $\rho_{11}=0.5,\ 0.3352,\ 0.2247,\ 0.0677$ and $\vert\rho_{01}\vert=0.5,\ 0.3033,\ 0.1839,\ 0.0410$, equal to the closed-form formulas to four digits. At time 20, $\vert\rho_{01}\vert=0.3033$, matching the 0.303 of the hand calculation.

blocks.title: Check yourself: reading the spectrum
blocks.text: A single qubit has Liouvillian eigenvalues $0,\ -0.1,\ -0.15\pm0.5i$. What are $T_1$, $T_2$, the Larmor frequency and the gap? After how long has the population mode shrunk by a factor of 100?
blocks.hint: The real parts are the rates; the imaginary parts are frequencies.
solution: The population mode decays at $1/T_1=0.1$, so $T_1=10$.
The coherence pair is $-1/T_2\pm i\omega$, so $T_2=1/0.15=6.67$ and $\omega=0.5$. Check $T_2\le2T_1=20$ ✓.
The gap is the smallest decay rate, $\min(0.1,0.15)=0.1$.

blocks.text: Several qubits: balancing the Hamiltonian against the damping

Take the two coupled, damped qubits $H=J\,X_1X_2+h\,(Z_1+Z_2)$ with $J=h=1$, and amplitude damping at rate $\gamma$ on each. One might guess the steady state is $\vert00\rangle$, everything relaxed to the ground state, but that is wrong. The coupling $X_1X_2$ contains pair-creation terms, $\sigma^+_1\sigma^+_2+\sigma^-_1\sigma^-_2$ (plus the number-conserving ones), which keep pumping excitations in against the damping. The steady state is the compromise of the two, and it is just the null vector of $\hat{\mathcal L}$.

blocks.source:
import numpy as np
from scipy.linalg import expm
I = np.eye(2); X = np.array([[0, 1], [1, 0]]); Z = np.diag([1., -1.])
sm = np.array([[0, 1], [0, 0]])          # sigma^- = |0><1| (|1> is the excited state)

def kron(*ops):
    out = np.array([[1.]])
    for o in ops: out = np.kron(out, o)
    return out

def liouvillian(H, jumps):
    d = H.shape[0]; Id = np.eye(d)
    L = -1j * (np.kron(H, Id) - np.kron(Id, H.T))
    for c in jumps:
        cdc = c.conj().T @ c
        L += np.kron(c, c.conj()) - 0.5 * np.kron(cdc, Id) - 0.5 * np.kron(Id, cdc.T)
    return L

J, h = 1.0, 1.0
H = J * kron(X, X) + h * (kron(Z, I) + kron(I, Z))
for gamma in [0.1, 0.4]:
    L = liouvillian(H, [np.sqrt(gamma) * kron(sm, I), np.sqrt(gamma) * kron(I, sm)])
    ev = np.linalg.eigvals(L); ev = ev[np.argsort(-ev.real)]
    gap = -ev.real[1]
    print(f"gamma = {gamma}: slowest rates -Re(lambda) = {np.round(-ev.real[:5], 4)}, gap {gap:.4f}, relaxation time {1/gap:.1f}")
    w, v = np.linalg.eig(L)
    ss = v[:, np.argmin(abs(w))].reshape(4, 4); ss /= np.trace(ss)
    print("   steady-state populations |00>,|01>,|10>,|11>:", np.round(np.diag(ss).real, 4), " trace", np.round(np.trace(ss).real, 4))
    rho0 = np.zeros((4, 4)); rho0[3, 3] = 1
    rhoT = (expm(L * 300) @ rho0.reshape(-1)).reshape(4, 4)
    print("   rho(t=300) from |11> matches steady state:", np.allclose(rhoT, ss, atol=1e-6))

blocks.text: The output: for $\gamma=0.1$ the slowest decay rates are 0.0553 (four-fold degenerate), a relaxation time of 18.1 time units, a little shorter than the 20 you would get from the isolated-qubit coherence rate $\gamma/2=0.05$ (the slowest modes are coherences, which decay at half the population rate). The steady-state populations of $\vert00\rangle,\vert01\rangle,\vert10\rangle,\vert11\rangle$ are $0.8501,\ 0.05,\ 0.05,\ 0.05$: far from $\vert00\rangle$. For $\gamma=0.4$ the gap is 0.2217, about four times larger ($0.2217/0.0553=4.0$), in proportion to $\gamma$; the relaxation time is 4.5; and the steady state is almost the same ($0.8512,0.0496,\dots$, a change in the third decimal). So here the damping rate sets how fast the system settles, while the Hamiltonian-against-damping balance sets where it settles. Starting from $\vert11\rangle$ and waiting 300 time units gives the steady state to six digits.

This is the typical shape of a driven-dissipative reservoir: a non-trivial steady state set by the competition between the Hamiltonian and the jumps, relaxation at a rate set mostly by the damping, and, once the Hamiltonian depends on an input $s$, a steady state that carries the input.
Heating: a quick steady-state calculation

One more exact result is worth having. With both energy loss ($\sigma^-$ at rate $\gamma_\downarrow$) and heating ($\sigma^+$ at rate $\gamma_\uparrow$) and no Hamiltonian, the excited population obeys $\dot\rho_{11}=-\gamma_\downarrow\rho_{11}+\gamma_\uparrow\rho_{00}=\gamma_\uparrow-(\gamma_\downarrow+\gamma_\uparrow)\rho_{11}$, because $\rho_{00}=1-\rho_{11}$. It relaxes to $\rho_{11}^*=\gamma_\uparrow/(\gamma_\uparrow+\gamma_\downarrow)$ at rate $\gamma_\uparrow+\gamma_\downarrow$. With $\gamma_\downarrow=0.1$ and $\gamma_\uparrow=0.02$: $\rho_{11}^*=0.02/0.12=0.167$ and the rate is $0.12$, so the heating both limits the steady state and speeds up the approach to it.
Discrete steps from continuous dynamics

Reservoir models are usually written in discrete time: input $s_k$ arrives, the system evolves for $\Delta t$, the features are read. With a Lindbladian the step is $\mathcal T_s=e^{\Delta t\,\mathcal L(s)}$, possibly composed with an input-writing channel such as the reset of Density Matrices and Channels (#/qrc/open-systems/density-matrices-and-channels). A gap $g$ then contracts the deviation from the steady state by about $e^{-g\Delta t}$ per step, so the memory is about $1/(g\Delta t)$ steps. Two cautions. First, with a different Liouvillian $\mathcal L(s)$ at each step, the steady state moves with $s$, and what the reservoir remembers is a smoothed-out record of where the steady state has been. The non-commutation of $\mathcal L(s)$ at different $s$ is where nonlinear memory comes from. Second, the contraction of a product of channels is not the product of the gaps: the next page, Contraction and Fixed Points (#/qrc/open-systems/contraction-and-fixed-points), handles that.

This is the knob that Sannia and co-authors tune in Dissipation as a Resource (#/qrc/models/dissipation-as-resource): adding tunable local losses to a spin reservoir supplies fading memory without any reset, reproduces the reset-based models, and improves linear and nonlinear memory tasks and the forecast of chaotic series.

blocks.title: Check yourself: memory in steps
blocks.text: A reservoir has Liouvillian gap $g=0.2217$ and each step lasts $\Delta t=0.5$. Roughly how many steps until a perturbation has shrunk by $e^3\approx20$?
blocks.hint: Multiply the gap by the step length first.
solution: Per step the deviation shrinks by $e^{-g\Delta t}=e^{-0.1109}$.

blocks.text: Quantum trajectories
Why bother

The master equation describes the average state of many identical systems. A single system observed in its environment (a device that watches the emitted photons) follows a random path: it evolves smoothly for a while and occasionally jumps. This is also a practical simulation method: $M$ trajectories of pure states cost memory of order $d$ instead of the $d^2$ of a density matrix, with a statistical error of order $1/\sqrt M$.
The recipe and why it works

Our short-time Kraus operators already contain the recipe. Over $dt$, a state $\vert\psi\rangle$ goes either to $K_0\vert\psi\rangle$ or to $K_j\vert\psi\rangle$. The chance of a jump $j$ is $\Vert K_j\psi\Vert^2=\gamma_j\,dt\,\Vert L_j\psi\Vert^2$. So: evolve with the non-Hermitian effective Hamiltonian $H_{\mathrm{eff}}=H-\tfrac i2\sum_j\gamma_jL_j^\dagger L_j$ (the norm falls by exactly the probability that a jump happened), and at random times apply a jump $\psi\to L_j\psi/\Vert L_j\psi\Vert$. Averaging $\vert\psi\rangle\langle\psi\vert$ over many runs reproduces $\rho(t)$, because each step is the Kraus map of the previous section, applied in a way that keeps a record of the 'which Kraus operator' choice. A single trajectory's pure state is the state of an observer who sees every jump. The master equation is the state of an observer who sees none.

The next program simulates a driven, decaying qubit ($H=\tfrac12\Omega X$ and $\sigma^-$ at rate 0.3) with 1000 trajectories, and compares $\langle Z\rangle$ against the exact result from the Liouvillian.

blocks.source:
import numpy as np
from scipy.linalg import expm
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
X = np.array([[0, 1], [1, 0]], complex); Z = np.diag([1., -1]).astype(complex); sm = np.array([[0, 1], [0, 0]], complex)
Om, gam, dt, T = 1.0, 0.3, 0.01, 10.0            # H = (Om/2) X, jump sigma^- at rate gam
H = 0.5 * Om * X
Heff = H - 0.5j * gam * sm.conj().T @ sm
Ueff = expm(-1j * Heff * dt)
steps = int(T / dt); M = 1000
zs = np.zeros(steps)
for m in range(M):
    psi = np.array([1, 0], complex)               # start in |0>
    for k in range(steps):
        psi = Ueff @ psi                          # no-jump evolution (norm shrinks)
        pjump = 1 - np.vdot(psi, psi).real        # probability a jump happened in dt
        if rng.random() < pjump:
            psi = sm @ psi                        # jump
        psi /= np.linalg.norm(psi)
        zs[k] += np.vdot(psi, Z @ psi).real
zs /= M
# exact master equation by vectorisation
Id = np.eye(2)
L = -1j * (np.kron(H, Id) - np.kron(Id, H.T)) + gam * (np.kron(sm, sm.conj()) - 0.5 * np.kron(sm.conj().T @ sm, Id) - 0.5 * np.kron(Id, (sm.conj().T @ sm).T))
rho0 = np.array([[1, 0], [0, 0]], complex).reshape(-1)
for t in [1, 3, 6, 10]:
    r = (expm(L * t) @ rho0).reshape(2, 2)
    print(f"t = {t:4.1f}: <Z> master equation {np.trace(Z @ r).real:+.4f}   {M} trajectories {zs[int(t/dt)-1]:+.4f}")

blocks.text: The output: at $t=1,3,6,10$ the master equation gives $\langle Z\rangle=+0.6026,\ -0.4223,\ +0.2635,\ -0.0549$ and the trajectory average gives $+0.6026,\ -0.4232,\ +0.2533,\ -0.0902$. The agreement is within about $0.03$ even at the end, the size of the statistical error $\sim1/\sqrt{1000}$. The curve is a damped Rabi oscillation, relaxing toward the steady state $\langle Z\rangle\approx0$ of the driven, damped qubit. The trajectory picture is also what a device that monitors its environment would see, which is the bridge to measurement-based protocols on Online Measurement Protocols (#/qrc/hardware/online-protocols).
Putting it together: the memory budget of a real qubit
A reservoir is built from superconducting qubits with $T_1=50\ \mu s$ and $T_2=40\ \mu s$ and a step of $\Delta t=1\ \mu s$. We want to know how many steps its natural noise allows.

items: Step 1. Per-step amplitude damping: $\gamma=1-e^{-1/50}=0.0198$.

Step 2. Per-step coherence factor: $e^{-1/40}=0.9753$. As dephasing alone that is $p=0.0123$; part of the loss, $\sqrt{1-\gamma}=0.9901$, is already inside the amplitude damping, so the extra pure dephasing is a factor $0.9753/0.9901=0.9851$.
Step 3. Memory length for populations: $T_1/\Delta t=50$ steps to fall to $1/e$; for coherences $T_2/\Delta t=40$ steps. Coherence-carried memory goes first.
Step 4. To fall by a factor 1000 (a typical 'forgotten' level) takes $\ln1000$ times these: 345 steps for populations and 276 for coherences.

Step 5. So any reservoir on this hardware that needs memory beyond a few hundred steps must reckon with the noise as a source of unwanted contraction; and as a resource, it supplies the fading memory for free (the next page returns to this).

blocks.text: Key points

items: The Lindblad equation $\dot\rho=-i[H,\rho]+\sum_j\gamma_j(L_j\rho L_j^\dagger-\tfrac12\{L_j^\dagger L_j,\rho\})$ is the continuous-time limit of channels made of a no-jump and a jump Kraus operator; $\gamma_j\ge0$ guarantees complete positivity.
The dissipator terms cancel in the trace, so $\operatorname{Tr}\rho$ stays 1. The anticommutator is the effect of no jump having occurred.
For a qubit, populations decay at $1/T_1$ and coherences at $1/T_2$ with $1/T_2=1/(2T_1)+1/T_\varphi$, so $T_2\le2T_1$.
Per reservoir step of length $\Delta t$: $\gamma=1-e^{-\Delta t/T_1}$, and coherence factor $e^{-\Delta t/T_2}$.

Vectorising gives the Liouvillian matrix $\hat{\mathcal L}$ via $\operatorname{vec}(A\rho B)=(A\otimes B^\top)\operatorname{vec}\rho$. Its zero eigenvector is the steady state; the smallest nonzero decay rate is the gap $g$, and the memory is about $1/(g\Delta t)$ steps.
A Hamiltonian competing with damping gives a non-trivial steady state, not the ground state.
Quantum trajectories (no-jump evolution with $H_{\mathrm{eff}}$ plus random jumps) average to the master equation.

blocks.text: Problems

blocks.title: Pure dephasing time
blocks.text: A qubit has $T_1=50\ \mu s$ and $T_2=40\ \mu s$. Find $T_\varphi$. Starting in $\vert+\rangle$, what is $\vert\rho_{01}\vert$ after $20\ \mu s$? Starting in $\vert1\rangle$, what is $\langle Z\rangle$ then?

blocks.title: Damping per reservoir step
blocks.text: A reservoir step lasts $\Delta t=1\ \mu s$ on qubits with $T_1=50\ \mu s$. What amplitude-damping parameter does one step apply, and after how many steps has an excited population fallen to $1/e$?
solution: Each step multiplies the excited population by $1-\gamma=e^{-0.02}$; reaching $1/e$ takes $T_1/\Delta t=50$ steps.

blocks.title: Memory horizon from the gap
blocks.text: The two-qubit example at $\gamma=0.1$ has gap $0.0553$. If the reservoir is sampled every $\Delta t=1$, roughly how many steps until a perturbation has shrunk by $e^3\approx20$? What about $\gamma=0.4$ (gap $0.2217$)?
solution: For $\gamma=0.4$: $3/0.2217=13.5$ steps. A four times stronger damping gives a four times shorter memory.
So the washout should be at least about 54 (or 14) steps.

blocks.title: A steady state with heating
blocks.text: A qubit with no Hamiltonian has $\sigma^-$ at rate $\gamma_\downarrow=0.1$ and $\sigma^+$ at rate $\gamma_\uparrow=0.02$. Find the steady-state excited population and the time to approach it. Starting from $\rho_{11}=0$, what is $\rho_{11}$ at $t=10$?

blocks.title: From the Kraus operators to the equation
blocks.text: Show that the dephasing dissipator $\gamma_\varphi/2$ with $L=Z$ is what you get by applying $Z$ with probability $p=\gamma_\varphi dt/2$ in a short time $dt$.
blocks.hint: For small $dt$, compare the coefficient of $dt$.
solution: The Lindblad term with $L=Z$ and rate $\gamma=\gamma_\varphi/2$ is $\gamma(Z\rho Z-\tfrac12Z^2\rho-\tfrac12\rho Z^2)=\gamma(Z\rho Z-\rho)$ since $Z^2=I$. The two agree.
The coherence then obeys $\dot\rho_{01}=\tfrac{\gamma_\varphi}2(-2)\rho_{01}=-\gamma_\varphi\rho_{01}$, as used above.

items: The next page, Contraction and Fixed Points (#/qrc/open-systems/contraction-and-fixed-points), turns the gap and the channel spectrum into the contraction and fixed-point conditions behind the echo state property.
The page Measurement (#/qrc/open-systems/measurement) is the third kind of environment: an ignored measurement is also a channel.

On the Models shelf, Dissipation as a Resource (#/qrc/models/dissipation-as-resource) and Dynamical Regimes (#/qrc/models/dynamical-regimes) use the Lindbladian as a tunable resource; on the Hardware shelf, Gate-Based Devices (#/qrc/hardware/gate-based-devices) meets T1 and T2 in real devices.
